messages.content: Write the product page copy for a team chat application, aimed at engineering managers who are choosing between tools. Around 250 words.

output:
Product name and all figures are invented placeholders — swap in your real numbers before this ships.

---

**Ferry — team chat for people who ship**

Most chat tools are built for the person sending the message. Ferry is built for the twelve people who have to read it.

**Threads that end.** Every thread carries a status: open, answered, or archived. An answered thread stops pinging. Nobody scrolls back through 400 messages to find out whether the deploy question ever got resolved — it's marked, with the answer pinned at the top.

**One channel per service, not per feeling.** Ferry maps channels to your repos and services. When `#payments-api` goes quiet for a sprint, it tells you. When it lights up at 2am, the on-call rotation is already in the header, and the page goes out from the same place the conversation started.

**Search that knows what code is.** Paste a stack trace, get the three threads where someone else hit it. Ferry indexes code blocks separately from prose, so `NullPointerException` doesn't match every message containing the word "null."

**What you'll notice in week one:**

- Notification volume drops. In our beta, median unread count per engineer fell from 180/day to 34.
- Migration from Slack takes an afternoon. History, files, and channel structure come across; DMs stay private.
- $7/user/month. No enterprise tier, no sales call.

Ferry won't make your team communicate better. It will stop the tool from making it worse, and it will tell you which channels are dead so you can close them.

[Start a 30-day trial] · [Read the migration guide]

---

~250 words. Three things I'd flag for your review: the beta notification numbers need a real source before you publish them, the Slack-migration claim commits you to importing files and channel structure, and the "no sales call" line rules out an enterprise motion later.
